name: Pineal gland
func: A tiny gland deep in the middle of the brain that makes melatonin, mostly at night. Melatonin tells the body it is dark, helping set the daily sleep–wake rhythm.

levels.kid:
The **pineal gland** is a teeny gland deep in the very middle of your brain. It is shaped like a little **pine cone**, which is how it got its name.

Its job is to help you know when it is time to **sleep**. When it gets dark outside, your eyes notice, and a message travels to the pineal gland. The pineal gland then makes a sleepy chemical called **melatonin**.

Melatonin is like a soft whisper that says, "It's nighttime, time to rest." In the morning when the sun comes up, the pineal gland makes less, and you wake up ready to play.
levels.hs:
The **pineal gland** is a small, reddish-gray gland about **8 mm** long, shaped like a pine cone. It sits in the middle of the brain, attached to the back of the **roof of the third ventricle** by a short stalk. It lies just above the **superior colliculi** of the midbrain and below the **splenium** of the corpus callosum, in a space surrounded by large deep veins, including the **great cerebral vein (of Galen)**. It is one of the few brain structures that is **unpaired**.

Its main product is **melatonin**, a hormone made from **serotonin**, which comes from the amino acid **tryptophan**. Melatonin levels rise in the evening, peak in the middle of the night and fall by morning. It acts as a timing signal that helps align body rhythms like sleep, body temperature and other hormone cycles with day and night.

The pineal gland often builds up **calcium deposits** with age, called "brain sand." These show up as a bright dot on CT scans and X-rays and can be used as a midline landmark.

The philosopher **Descartes** famously thought the pineal gland was the seat of the soul, because it is single and central.
levels.college:
The pineal gland develops as an outpouching of the roof of the **diencephalon** and is part of the **epithalamus**, along with the **habenular nuclei**. Its stalk has a superior lamina, containing the **habenular commissure**, and an inferior lamina, containing the **posterior commissure**; between them is the **pineal recess** of the third ventricle.

It is a **circumventricular organ**: its capillaries are fenestrated, so it lies largely outside the blood–brain barrier. Blood comes mainly from branches of the **medial posterior choroidal arteries**, and it drains into the internal cerebral veins and the vein of Galen.

The main cells are **pinealocytes**, supported by astrocyte-like interstitial cells.

The control pathway is surprisingly long. Light hits **melanopsin**-containing retinal ganglion cells → **retinohypothalamic tract** → **suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN)** of the hypothalamus → **paraventricular nucleus** → descending fibers to the **intermediolateral cell column** of the upper thoracic spinal cord → **superior cervical ganglion** → postganglionic **sympathetic fibers** that climb along blood vessels back into the skull to the pineal. At night, these fibers release **noradrenaline**, which acts on **beta-1 adrenergic receptors** to switch on melatonin synthesis.

Because of this sympathetic route, damage to the cervical sympathetic chain can disrupt melatonin rhythms.

Melatonin acts on **MT1** and **MT2** receptors, including those in the SCN itself, forming a feedback loop that helps shift the body clock.
levels.phd:
Melatonin synthesis occurs in four steps: tryptophan → 5-hydroxytryptophan (**tryptophan hydroxylase**) → serotonin (**aromatic amino acid decarboxylase**) → N-acetylserotonin (**arylalkylamine N-acetyltransferase, AANAT**) → melatonin (**acetylserotonin O-methyltransferase, ASMT**, formerly HIOMT). AANAT is the **rate-limiting "timezyme"**: noradrenaline acting via beta-1 receptors raises cAMP, which activates PKA. In rodents this strongly increases AANAT gene transcription through CREB, while in primates the main control is post-translational: phosphorylation lets **14-3-3 proteins** bind and protect AANAT from rapid proteasomal destruction. When lights come on at night, AANAT is degraded within minutes, so melatonin falls quickly.

Melatonin is not stored; it diffuses out as it is made, so blood levels track synthesis closely. Its duration encodes **night length**, which in seasonal mammals acts as a yearly calendar (for coat change, fat storage and hibernation) via MT1 receptors in the pars tuberalis of the pituitary, a field known as **photoperiodism**.

**MT1 and MT2** are G protein-coupled receptors (mainly Gi). In the SCN, MT1 activation suppresses neuronal firing, and MT2 helps phase-shift the clock. Melatonin also has antioxidant properties in experimental systems, though their importance in humans is uncertain.

In non-mammalian vertebrates the pineal is directly **photosensitive** (a "third eye"). Some reptiles, such as the tuatara, have a **parietal eye** with a lens and retina-like layer. Mammals lost direct photoreception, and pinealocytes evolved from photoreceptor-like cells, which explains shared genes such as those of the phototransduction cascade.
levels.expert:
Clinically, the pineal matters mostly because of **where** it is, not what it makes.

**Pineal region tumors** include **germ cell tumors** (especially **germinoma**, most common in teenage boys and highly sensitive to radiotherapy and chemotherapy), **pineal parenchymal tumors** (pineocytoma, slow-growing, through **pineoblastoma**, a malignant embryonal tumor of childhood), gliomas and meningiomas. They present with:
- **Obstructive hydrocephalus** from compression of the **cerebral aqueduct**: headache, vomiting and papilledema.
- **Parinaud (dorsal midbrain) syndrome** from pressure on the tectum: upgaze palsy, **light–near dissociation**, convergence–retraction nystagmus and **Collier sign** (lid retraction).

Workup: **MRI** of the brain and whole spine (for spread), serum and CSF **tumor markers** (such as AFP) and CSF cytology. Markers can diagnose some germ cell tumors without biopsy.

Neurosurgical approaches: hydrocephalus is often treated first with an **endoscopic third ventriculostomy**, during which a **biopsy** can be taken. Resection uses the **supracerebellar infratentorial** route (Krause), working under the tentorium above the cerebellum, or the **occipital transtentorial** route (Poppen). The deep venous system, especially the **vein of Galen** and **internal cerebral veins**, must be protected.

**Pineal cysts** are common incidental findings on MRI; most are harmless and need no treatment. Pineal **calcification** in a young child is unusual and may prompt a closer look. Melatonin itself is used medically for some circadian rhythm sleep disorders and jet lag, under medical guidance.

keyPoints: Tiny unpaired gland in the epithalamus, behind the third ventricle, above the superior colliculi
Makes melatonin from serotonin, mostly at night
Control path: retina → SCN → PVN → spinal cord → superior cervical ganglion → pineal
Calcifies with age ('brain sand'), a midline landmark on CT
Pineal tumors → hydrocephalus and Parinaud syndrome

test.q: Melatonin is made from which molecule?
The hypothalamic master clock that controls the pineal is the ______ nucleus.
test.explain: The SCN receives light information from the retina and drives the pineal through a sympathetic pathway.

test.q: A pineal tumor causing upgaze palsy and light–near dissociation produces:
test.explain: Compression of the dorsal midbrain (tectum) causes Parinaud syndrome.

test.q: At night, which transmitter from sympathetic nerves switches on melatonin production?
test.explain: Noradrenaline acts on beta-1 receptors on pinealocytes, raising cAMP and AANAT activity.

test.q: Age-related calcium deposits in the pineal are nicknamed brain ______.
test.explain: Corpora arenacea show up as a bright midline dot on CT.
